Deploy Paperless-ngx on a NAS (OCR Document Archive) — Build a Homelab Skip to content Script
 bash > docker-compose.env Copy 
 # Deploy Paperless-ngx (OCR document management) with Docker Compose.
# Full walkthrough + the acceptance test: /articles/paperless-ngx-document-archive
# Requires Docker + Compose v2 on the host (a NAS or small always-on server).
# 1. Run the OFFICIAL interactive installer. It asks about database, broker,
# folders and ports, then writes a ready-to-run compose project.
bash -c "$(curl -L https://raw.githubusercontent.com/paperless-ngx/paperless-ngx/main/install-paperless-ngx.sh)"
# - Database: SQLite is fine for a single-user archive (one fewer container,
# single-file backups). Choose PostgreSQL if you expect many users / heavy ingest.
# - Broker: a Redis-compatible service; the current official compose uses Valkey.
# 2. In the generated docker-compose.yml, PIN the image to a real release.
# GHCR DROPS the release 'v' prefix: use 3.0.5, NOT v3.0.5 (v = manifest unknown).
# Check https://github.com/paperless-ngx/paperless-ngx/releases for the current tag.
# image: ghcr.io/paperless-ngx/paperless-ngx:3.0.5
# 3. In the generated env file, set allowed hosts + trusted origins. Django treats
# localhost and 127.0.0.1 as DIFFERENT hosts, so list BOTH plus every real address.
cat >> docker-compose.env <<'EOF'
PAPERLESS_ALLOWED_HOSTS=localhost,127.0.0.1,10.0.0.50,paperless.homelab.lan
PAPERLESS_CSRF_TRUSTED_ORIGINS=http://localhost:8020,http://127.0.0.1:8020,http://10.0.0.50:8020
PAPERLESS_ADMIN_USER=youradmin
# Set PAPERLESS_ADMIN_PASSWORD from your secret store before first boot, not here.
EOF
# 4. Bring it up.
docker compose pull
docker compose up -d
# 5. ACCEPTANCE TEST (the honest one): feed it an IMAGE-ONLY PDF with no text
# layer, so OCR is the only way any text can exist, then search for a word
# printed only in the image. If it's found, ingest + OCR + search all work.
# - Drop the image-only PDF into the consume folder (e.g. ./consume/).
# - Wait for it to disappear (ingested), then search that word in the UI.
 What this does
 This deploys Paperless-ngx — a self-hosted document management system with OCR — using its official interactive installer, which generates a Docker Compose project. Once running, you drop PDFs or scanned images into a watched consume folder and Paperless runs Tesseract OCR to make the text searchable. It’s an ideal service for a NAS , where your documents and backups already live.
 The full walkthrough, including the two Django gotchas and the acceptance test, is in Paperless-ngx: OCR Every Document You Own, Searchable .
 Prerequisites
 A host with Docker and the Docker Compose v2 plugin — a NAS that supports Docker, or a small Linux server.
 Enough disk for your documents plus their OCR’d copies and thumbnails. Documents are the point; give them room.
 Somewhere to keep the admin password — a password manager, not a note.
 Notes
 Make these values your own before you rely on the result: replace 10.0.0.50 with your Paperless host’s real IP, paperless.homelab.lan with your real hostname, youradmin with your chosen admin username, and set the admin password from your secret store (never paste a real password into the env file in a repo). Add any Tailscale or LAN address you’ll use to the allowed-hosts list. If a value looks specific to one machine, it’s a placeholder to change, not a literal to copy.
 The GHCR tag has no v . Releases are named v3.0.5 ; the container tag is 3.0.5 . Using :v3.0.5 yields manifest unknown . Pin a real release and re-check the releases page before bumping.
 localhost ≠ 127.0.0.1 to Django. List both in PAPERLESS_ALLOWED_HOSTS (and matching PAPERLESS_CSRF_TRUSTED_ORIGINS ) or a login/POST can 400 — which is easy to misread as an ingestion failure when documents are actually importing fine. PAPERLESS_URL can set these together per the configuration docs .
 SQLite vs PostgreSQL is a real choice. SQLite is simplest for one user and backs up as a single file; PostgreSQL scales better for many users or heavy ingestion. You can migrate later .
 Back up data/ and media/ from day one. These hold your archive; put them in your backup scope before importing anything you can’t afford to lose.
 Trust the forced-OCR acceptance test, not the loading UI. A web page that loads only proves the web server runs. An image-only PDF whose printed text becomes searchable proves ingest, OCR, and search all work end to end.

Installation

Quick Start

If you just want Paperless-ngx running quickly, use our installation script:

bash -c "$(curl --location --silent --show-error https://raw.githubusercontent.com/paperless-ngx/paperless-ngx/main/install-paperless-ngx.sh)"

If piping into a shell directly from the internet makes you nervous, inspect the script first!

Overview

Choose the installation route that best fits your setup:

Route	Best for	Effort
Installation script	Fastest first-time setup with guided prompts (recommended for most users)	Low
Docker Compose templates	Manual control over compose files and settings	Medium
Bare metal	Advanced setups, packaging, and development-adjacent workflows	High
Hosted providers (wiki)	Managed hosting options maintained by the community — check details carefully	Varies

For most users, Docker is the best option. It is faster to set up, easier to maintain, and ships with sensible defaults.

The bare-metal route gives you more control, but it requires manual installation and operation of all components. It is usually best suited for advanced users and contributors.

Info

Because superuser accounts have full access to all objects and documents, you may want to create a separate user account for daily use, or "downgrade" your superuser account to a normal user account after setup.

Installation Script

Paperless-ngx provides an interactive script for Docker Compose setups. It asks a few configuration questions, then creates the required files, pulls the image, starts the containers, and creates your superuser account. In short, it automates the Docker Compose setup described below.

Prerequisites
Docker and Docker Compose must be installed.
macOS users will need GNU sed with support for running as sed as well as wget.
Run the installation script
bash -c "$(curl --location --silent --show-error https://raw.githubusercontent.com/paperless-ngx/paperless-ngx/main/install-paperless-ngx.sh)"

After installation

Paperless-ngx should be available at http://127.0.0.1:8000 (or similar, depending on your configuration) and you will be able to login with the credentials you provided during the installation script.

Docker Compose Install
Prerequisites
Docker and Docker Compose must be installed.
Installation

Go to the /docker/compose directory on the project page and download one docker-compose.*.yml file for your preferred database backend. Save it in a local directory as docker-compose.yml. Also download docker-compose.env and .env into that same directory.

If you want to enable optional support for Office and other documents, download a file with -tika in the file name.

Tip

For new installations, it is recommended to use PostgreSQL as the database backend.

Modify docker-compose.yml as needed. For example, you may want to change the paths for consume, media, and other directories to use bind mounts. Find the line that specifies where to mount the directory, e.g.:

- ./consume:/usr/src/paperless/consume


Replace the part before the colon with your local directory:

- /home/jonaswinkler/paperless-inbox:/usr/src/paperless/consume


You may also want to change the default port that the webserver will use from the default (8000) to something else, e.g. for port 8010:

ports:
  - 8010:8000


Modify docker-compose.env with any configuration options you need. See the configuration documentation for all options.

You may also need to set USERMAP_UID and USERMAP_GID to the UID and GID of your user on the host system. Use id -u and id -g to get these values. This ensures both the container and the host user can write to the consumption directory. If your UID and GID are 1000 (the default for the first normal user on many systems), this usually works out of the box without modifications. Run id "username" to check.

Note

You can utilize Docker secrets for configuration settings by appending _FILE to configuration values. For example PAPERLESS_DBUSER can be set using PAPERLESS_DBUSER_FILE=/var/run/secrets/password.txt.

Run docker compose pull. This pulls the image from the GitHub container registry by default, but you can pull from Docker Hub by changing the image line to image: paperlessngx/paperless-ngx:latest.

Run docker compose up -d. This will create and start the necessary containers.

After installation

Your Paperless-ngx instance should now be accessible at http://127.0.0.1:8000 (or similar, depending on your configuration). When you first access the web interface, you will be prompted to create a superuser account.

Optional Advanced Compose Configurations

Rootless

Warning

It is not possible to run the container rootless if additional languages are specified via PAPERLESS_OCR_LANGUAGES.

If you want to run Paperless as a rootless container, set user: in docker-compose.yml to the UID and GID of your host user (use id -u and id -g to find these values). The container process starts directly as that user with no internal privilege remapping. Any UID and GID is supported:

webserver:
  image: ghcr.io/paperless-ngx/paperless-ngx:latest
  user: '1000:1000'


Do not combine this with USERMAP_UID or USERMAP_GID, which are intended for the non-rootless case described in step 3.

File systems without inotify support (e.g. NFS)

Some file systems, such as NFS network shares, don't support file system notifications with inotify. When the consumption directory is on such a file system, Paperless-ngx will not pick up new files with the default configuration. Set PAPERLESS_CONSUMER_POLLING_INTERVAL to a positive number to enable polling and disable native filesystem notifications.

Bare Metal Install
Prerequisites
Paperless runs on Linux only, Windows is not supported.
Python 3.11, 3.12, 3.13, or 3.14 is required. As a policy, Paperless-ngx aims to support at least the three most recent Python versions and drops support for versions as they reach end-of-life. Newer versions may work, but some dependencies may not be fully compatible.
Installation

Install dependencies. Paperless requires the following packages:

python3
python3-pip
python3-dev
default-libmysqlclient-dev for MariaDB
pkg-config for mysqlclient (python dependency)
fonts-liberation for generating thumbnails for plain text files
gnupg for decrypting GPG-encrypted email
libpq-dev for PostgreSQL
libmagic-dev for mime type detection
mariadb-client for MariaDB compile time
poppler-utils for thumbnail generation and barcode detection

Use this list for your preferred package management:

python3 python3-pip python3-dev fonts-liberation gnupg libpq-dev default-libmysqlclient-dev pkg-config libmagic-dev poppler-utils


These dependencies are required for OCRmyPDF, which is used for text recognition. - unpaper - ghostscript - icc-profiles-free - qpdf - liblept5 - libxml2 - pngquant (suggested for certain PDF image optimizations) - zlib1g - tesseract-ocr >= 4.0.0 for OCR - tesseract-ocr language packs (tesseract-ocr-eng, tesseract-ocr-deu, etc)

Use this list for your preferred package management:

unpaper ghostscript icc-profiles-free qpdf liblept5 libxml2 pngquant zlib1g tesseract-ocr


On Raspberry Pi, these libraries are required as well: - libatlas-base-dev - libxslt1-dev - mime-support

You will also need these for installing some of the python dependencies: - build-essential - python3-setuptools - python3-wheel

Use this list for your preferred package management:

build-essential python3-setuptools python3-wheel


Install a Redis-compatible broker (a current release of Valkey or Redis) and configure it to start automatically.

Optional: Install postgresql and configure a database, user, and password for Paperless-ngx. If you do not wish to use PostgreSQL, MariaDB and SQLite are available as well.

Note

On bare-metal installations using SQLite, ensure the JSON1 extension is enabled. This is usually the case, but not always.

Create a system user with a new home folder in which you want to run Paperless-ngx.

adduser paperless --system --home /opt/paperless --group


Download a release archive from https://github.com/paperless-ngx/paperless-ngx/releases. For example:

curl -O -L https://github.com/paperless-ngx/paperless-ngx/releases/download/vX.Y.Z/paperless-ngx-vX.Y.Z.tar.xz


Extract the archive with

tar -xf paperless-ngx-vX.Y.Z.tar.xz


and copy the contents to the home directory of the user you created earlier (/opt/paperless).

Note

If you are updating an existing bare-metal installation rather than installing for the first time, see the bare metal update instructions instead -- extracting a new release on top of an old one can leave behind stale files from the previous version.

Optional: If you cloned the Git repository, you will need to compile the frontend yourself. See here and use the build step, not serve.

Configure Paperless-ngx. See configuration for details. Edit the included paperless.conf and adjust the settings to your needs. Required settings for getting Paperless-ngx running are:

PAPERLESS_REDIS should point to your broker, such as redis://localhost:6379.
PAPERLESS_DBENGINE should be one of postgresql, mariadb, or sqlite. PostgreSQL and MariaDB users must set this explicitly.
PAPERLESS_DBHOST should be the hostname on which your PostgreSQL server is running. Do not configure this to use SQLite instead. Also configure port, database name, user and password as necessary.
PAPERLESS_CONSUMPTION_DIR should point to the folder that Paperless-ngx should watch for incoming documents. Likewise, PAPERLESS_DATA_DIR and PAPERLESS_MEDIA_ROOT define where Paperless-ngx stores its data. If needed, these can point to the same directory.
PAPERLESS_SECRET_KEY should be a random sequence of characters. It's used for authentication. Failure to do so allows third parties to forge authentication credentials.
Set PAPERLESS_URL if you are behind a reverse proxy. This should point to your domain. Please see configuration for more information.

You can make many more adjustments, especially for OCR. The following options are recommended for most users: - Set PAPERLESS_OCR_LANGUAGE to the language most of your documents are written in. - Set PAPERLESS_TIME_ZONE to your local time zone.

Warning

Ensure your broker instance is secured.

Create the following directories if they do not already exist:

/opt/paperless/media
/opt/paperless/data
/opt/paperless/consume

Adjust these paths if you configured different folders. Then verify that the paperless user has write permissions:

ls -l -d /opt/paperless/media


If needed, change the owner with

sudo chown paperless:paperless /opt/paperless/media
sudo chown paperless:paperless /opt/paperless/data
sudo chown paperless:paperless /opt/paperless/consume


Install Python dependencies from requirements.txt.

sudo -Hu paperless pip3 install -r requirements.txt


This will install all Python dependencies in the home directory of the new paperless user.

Tip

You can use a virtual environment if you prefer. If you do, you may need to adjust the example scripts for your virtual environment paths.

Tip

If you use modern Python tooling, such as uv, installation will not include dependencies for PostgreSQL or MariaDB. You can select those extras with --extra <EXTRA>, or install all extras with --all-extras.

Go to /opt/paperless/src and execute the following command:

# This creates the database schema.
sudo -Hu paperless python3 manage.py migrate


Optional: Test that Paperless-ngx is working by running

# Manually starts the webserver
sudo -Hu paperless python3 manage.py runserver


Then point your browser to http://localhost:8000 if accessing from the same device on which Paperless-ngx is installed. If accessing from another machine, set up systemd services. You may need to set PAPERLESS_DEBUG=true in order for the development server to work normally in your browser.

Warning

This is a development server which should not be used in production. It is not audited for security, and performance is inferior to production-ready web servers.

Tip

This will not start the consumer. Paperless does this in a separate process.

Set up systemd services to run Paperless-ngx automatically. You may use the service definition files included in the scripts folder as a starting point.

Paperless needs: - The webserver script to run the webserver. - The consumer script to watch the input folder. - The taskqueue script for background workers (document consumption, etc.). - The scheduler script for periodic tasks such as email checking.

Note

The socket script enables granian to run on port 80 without root privileges. For this you need to uncomment the Require=paperless-webserver.socket in the webserver script and configure granian to listen on port 80 (set GRANIAN_PORT).

These services rely on the broker and optionally the database server, but don't need to be started in any particular order. The example files depend on the broker being started. If you use a database server, you should add additional dependencies.

Note

For instructions on using a reverse proxy, see the wiki.

Warning

If Celery won't start, check sudo systemctl status paperless-task-queue.service for paperless-task-queue.service and paperless-scheduler.service. You may need to change the path in the files. Example: ExecStart=/opt/paperless/.local/bin/celery --app paperless worker --loglevel INFO

Optional: Install the jbig2enc encoder. This will reduce the size of generated PDF documents. You'll most likely need to compile this yourself, because this software has been patented until around 2017 and binary packages are not available for most distributions.

After installation

Your Paperless-ngx instance should now be accessible at http://localhost:8000 (or similar, depending on your configuration). When you first access the web interface you will be prompted to create a superuser account.

Build the Docker image yourself

Building the Docker image yourself is typically used for development, but it can also be used for production if you want to customize the image. See Building the Docker image in the development documentation.

Migrating to Paperless-ngx

You can migrate to Paperless-ngx from Paperless-ng or from the original Paperless project.

Note

Upgrading an existing Paperless-ngx installation from v2 to v3 has its own breaking changes and required steps. See the v3 migration guide before upgrading.

Migrating from Paperless-ng

Paperless-ngx is meant to be a drop-in replacement for Paperless-ng, and upgrading should be trivial for most users, especially when using Docker. However, as with any major change, it is recommended to take a full backup first. Once you are ready, simply change the docker image to point to the new source. For example, if using Docker Compose, edit docker-compose.yml and change:

image: jonaswinkler/paperless-ng:latest


to

image: ghcr.io/paperless-ngx/paperless-ngx:latest


and then run docker compose up -d, which will pull the new image and recreate the container. That's it.

Users who installed with the bare-metal route should also update their Git clone to point to https://github.com/paperless-ngx/paperless-ngx, for example using: git remote set-url origin https://github.com/paperless-ngx/paperless-ngx and then pull the latest version.

Migrating from Paperless

At its core, Paperless-ngx is still Paperless and fully compatible. However, some things have changed under the hood, so you need to adapt your setup depending on how you installed Paperless.

This section describes how to update an existing Paperless Docker installation. Keep these points in mind:

Read the changelog and take note of breaking changes.
Decide whether to stay on SQLite or migrate to PostgreSQL. Both work fine with Paperless-ngx. However, if you already have a database server running for other services, you might as well use it for Paperless as well.
The task scheduler of Paperless, which is used to execute periodic tasks such as email checking and maintenance, requires a Redis-compatible message broker instance (such as Valkey or Redis). The Docker Compose route takes care of that.
The layout of the folder structure for your documents and data remains the same, so you can plug your old Docker volumes into paperless-ngx and expect it to find everything where it should be.

Migration to Paperless-ngx is then performed in a few simple steps:

Stop Paperless.

cd /path/to/current/paperless
docker compose down


Create a backup for two reasons: if something goes wrong, you still have your data; and if you don't like paperless-ngx, you can switch back to Paperless.

Download the latest release of Paperless-ngx. You can either use the Docker Compose files from here or clone the repository to build the image yourself (see development docs). You can either replace your current paperless folder or put Paperless-ngx in a different location.

Warning

Paperless-ngx includes a .env file. This will set the project name for Docker Compose to paperless, which will also define the volume names created by Paperless-ngx. However, if you notice that paperless-ngx is not using your old paperless volumes, verify the names of your volumes with

docker volume ls | grep _data


and adjust the project name in the .env file so that it matches the name of the volumes before the _data part.

Download the docker-compose.sqlite.yml file to docker-compose.yml. If you want to switch to PostgreSQL, do that after you migrated your existing SQLite database.

Adjust docker-compose.yml and docker-compose.env to your needs. See Docker setup for details on which edits are recommended.

Follow the update procedure in Update paperless.

In order to find your existing documents with the new search feature, you need to invoke a one-time operation that will create the search index:

docker compose run --rm webserver document_index reindex


This will migrate your database and create the search index. After that, Paperless-ngx will maintain the index automatically.

Start Paperless-ngx.

docker compose up -d


This will run Paperless-ngx in the background and automatically start it on system boot.

Paperless may have installed a permanent redirect to admin/ in your browser. This redirect is still in place and prevents access to the new UI. Clear your browser cache to fix this.

Optionally, follow the instructions below to migrate your existing data to PostgreSQL.

Migrating from LinuxServer.io Docker Image

As with any upgrade or large change, it is highly recommended to create a backup before starting. This assumes the image was running using Docker Compose, but the instructions are translatable to Docker commands as well.

Stop and remove the Paperless container.
If using an external database, stop that container.

Update broker configuration.

If REDIS_URL is already set, change it to PAPERLESS_REDIS and continue to step 4.

Otherwise, add a new broker service in docker-compose.yml, following the example compose files

Set the environment variable PAPERLESS_REDIS so it points to the new broker container.

Update user mapping.

If set, change the environment variable PUID to USERMAP_UID.

If set, change the environment variable PGID to USERMAP_GID.

Update configuration paths.

Set the environment variable PAPERLESS_DATA_DIR to /config.

Update media paths.

Set the environment variable PAPERLESS_MEDIA_ROOT to /data/media.

Update timezone.

Set the environment variable PAPERLESS_TIME_ZONE to the same value as TZ.

Modify image: to point to ghcr.io/paperless-ngx/paperless-ngx:latest or a specific version if preferred.

Start the containers as before, using docker compose.
Running Paperless-ngx on less powerful devices

Paperless runs on Raspberry Pi. Some tasks can be slow on lower-powered hardware, but a few settings can improve performance:

Stick with SQLite to save some resources. See troubleshooting if you encounter issues with SQLite locking.
If you do not need the filesystem-based consumer, consider disabling it entirely by setting PAPERLESS_CONSUMER_DISABLE to true.
Consider setting PAPERLESS_OCR_PAGES to 1, so that Paperless OCRs only the first page of your documents. In most cases, this page contains enough information to be able to find it.
PAPERLESS_TASK_WORKERS and PAPERLESS_THREADS_PER_WORKER are configured to use all cores. The Raspberry Pi models 3 and up have 4 cores, meaning that Paperless will use 2 workers and 2 threads per worker. This may result in sluggish response times during consumption, so you might want to lower these settings (example: 2 workers and 1 thread to always have some computing power left for other tasks).
Keep PAPERLESS_OCR_MODE at its default value auto and consider OCRing your documents before feeding them into Paperless. Some scanners are able to do this!
Set PAPERLESS_ARCHIVE_FILE_GENERATION to never to skip archive file generation entirely, saving disk space at the cost of in-browser PDF/A viewing.
If you want to perform OCR on the device, consider using PAPERLESS_OCR_CLEAN=none. This will speed up OCR times and use less memory at the expense of slightly worse OCR results.
If using Docker, consider setting PAPERLESS_WEBSERVER_WORKERS to 1. This will save some memory.

For details, refer to configuration.

Note

Updating the automatic matching algorithm takes quite a bit of time. However, the update mechanism checks if your data has changed before doing the heavy lifting. If you experience the algorithm taking too much CPU time, consider changing the schedule in the admin interface to daily. You can also manually invoke the task by changing the date and time of the next run to today/now.

The actual matching of the algorithm is fast and works on Raspberry Pi as well as on any other device.

Additional considerations

Using a reverse proxy with Paperless-ngx

Please see the wiki for user-maintained documentation on using nginx with Paperless-ngx.

Enhancing security

Please see the wiki for user-maintained documentation on configuring security tools like Fail2ban with Paperless-ngx.

Frequently Asked Questions
What's the general plan for Paperless-ngx?

A: While Paperless-ngx is already considered largely "feature-complete", it is a community-driven project and development will be guided in this way. New features can be submitted via GitHub discussions and "up-voted" by the community, but this is not a guarantee that the feature will be implemented. This project will always be open to collaboration in the form of PRs, ideas etc.

I'm using docker. Where are my documents?

A: By default, your documents are stored inside the docker volume paperless_media. Docker manages this volume automatically for you. It is a persistent storage and will persist as long as you don't explicitly delete it. The actual location depends on your host operating system. On Linux, chances are high that this location is

/var/lib/docker/volumes/paperless_media/_data


Warning

Do not mess with this folder. Don't change permissions and don't move files around manually. This folder is meant to be entirely managed by docker and paperless.

Note

Files consumed from the consumption directory are re-created inside this media directory and are removed from the consumption directory itself.

Let's say I want to switch tools in a year. Can I easily move to other systems?

A: Your documents are stored as plain files inside the media folder. You can always drag those files out of that folder to use them elsewhere. Here are a couple notes about that.

Paperless-ngx never modifies your original documents. It keeps checksums of all documents and uses a scheduled sanity checker to check that they remain the same.
By default, paperless uses the internal ID of each document as its filename. This might not be very convenient for export. However, you can adjust the way files are stored in paperless by configuring the filename format.
The exporter is another easy way to get your files out of paperless with reasonable file names.
What file types does paperless-ngx support?

A: Currently, the following files are supported:

PDF documents, PNG images, JPEG images, TIFF images, GIF images and WebP images are processed with OCR and converted into PDF documents.
Plain text documents are supported as well and are added verbatim to paperless.
With the optional Tika integration enabled (see Tika configuration), Paperless also supports various Office documents (.docx, .doc, odt, .ppt, .pptx, .odp, .xls, .xlsx, .ods).

Paperless-ngx determines the type of a file by inspecting its content rather than its file extensions. However, files processed via the consumption directory will be rejected if they have a file extension that is not supported by any of the available parsers.

Are duplicate documents rejected?

A: Not by default. As of v3, a file whose contents match an existing document is still consumed, and the duplicate is flagged in the UI — open the document and check the Duplicates tab to review documents that share the same content, or filter the document list by Duplicates to find all of them (see Duplicate documents). If you prefer the old behavior of rejecting duplicates during consumption, set PAPERLESS_CONSUMER_DELETE_DUPLICATES to true.

Will paperless-ngx run on Raspberry Pi?

A: The short answer is yes. I've tested it on a Raspberry Pi 3 B. The long answer is that certain parts of Paperless will run very slow, such as the OCR. On Raspberry Pi, try to OCR documents before feeding them into paperless so that paperless can reuse the text. The web interface is a lot snappier, since it runs in your browser and paperless has to do much less work to serve the data.

Note

You can adjust some of the settings so that paperless uses less processing power. See setup for details.

How do I install paperless-ngx on Raspberry Pi?

A: Docker images are available for arm64 hardware, so just follow the Docker Compose instructions. Apart from more required disk space compared to a bare metal installation, docker comes with close to zero overhead, even on Raspberry Pi.

If you decide to go with the bare metal route, be aware that some of the python requirements do not have precompiled packages for ARM / ARM64. Installation of these will require additional development libraries and compilation will take a long time.

Note

For ARMv7 (32-bit) systems, paperless may still function, but it could require modifications to the Dockerfile (if using Docker) or additional tools for installing bare metal. It is suggested to upgrade to arm64 instead.

How do I run this on Unraid?

A: Paperless-ngx is available as community app in Unraid. Uli Fahrer created a container template for that.

How do I run this on my toaster?

A: I honestly don't know! As for all other devices that might be able to run paperless, you're a bit on your own. If you can't run the docker image, the documentation has instructions for bare metal installs.

Does Paperless-ngx use AI, and is my data private?

A: Paperless-ngx includes optional AI features — LLM-based suggestions, document chat, and similar-document retrieval — that are disabled by default. They only run when you enable them and configure an LLM backend. The built-in tag/correspondent suggestions use a local, non-LLM machine-learning model and do not send your data anywhere. If you enable the LLM features, document content is sent to whichever backend you configure — this can be a fully local backend (e.g. Ollama) or a remote provider. See AI features for details.

Which message broker should I use?

Paperless-ngx talks to a Redis-compatible message broker, so any broker that implements the Redis protocol will work. The bundled Docker Compose files default to Valkey, the open-source fork created after Redis' licensing change, but Redis itself and other wire-compatible brokers (such as Microsoft's Garnet) are equally fine.

Existing installs can switch broker implementations in place: point PAPERLESS_REDIS at the new instance and reuse the same data volume.

 Best Docker containers to run on a Synology NAS in 2026 (7 picks)
 Synology's package store is smaller than what Docker unlocks. These seven containers cover photos, media, dashboards, and DNS with less RAM than most Synology apps use.
 Self-hosted 
 Open source 
 Free 
 Linux 
 No ads 
 Share 
 Synology’s Package Center covers photos, media, and file sync well, and it stops there. Container Manager (the rebranded Docker package on DSM 7.2) unlocks the whole open-source self-hosting catalogue with less RAM than most first-party Synology apps use for the same job. A DS923+ can happily run seven containers alongside file services once you disable Synology Drive and Moments, which nobody who uses Immich needs anyway.
 The seven best Docker containers to run on a Synology NAS below are the ones with the longest track record on DSM, the shortest first-run setup, and the clearest gains over the built-in Synology app. Container Manager on DSM 7.2 handles Docker Compose out of the box, so the config for each is a small YAML file you paste and start.
 What to look for in a Synology-friendly Docker container
 Amd64 image with an ARM64 variant for the value-line DS units.
 Bind mounts onto a Synology shared folder, so backups still go through Hyper Backup.
 A permission model that plays nicely with PUID / PGID set to your Synology user.
 Low memory footprint on models with 2–4 GB of RAM.
 A first-run wizard or a well-known reverse-proxy configuration.
 Active development , because DSM will keep changing under it.

 The apps
 1. Portainer – best container management UI
 Portainer turns Container Manager’s basic UI into a real Docker dashboard: environment variables, restart policies, network editing, live logs, and console access, all in a browser tab. If you plan to run more than three containers on your NAS, install Portainer first.
 Where it falls short: Business Edition adds RBAC and multi-cluster; the free Community Edition covers one Docker host well. Container Manager can still get confused about who is orchestrating what if you mix Portainer and DSM UI edits.
 Pricing: 
 Free: Community Edition, unlimited containers.
 Paid: Business Edition at $18/node/month.
 Platforms: Docker (Synology Container Manager).
 Download: Portainer.io 
 Bottom line: Portainer is the shell around every other container on this list.
 2. Immich – best Google Photos replacement
 Immich is the self-hosted photo library that finally feels like Google Photos. Mobile apps for iOS and Android auto-upload the camera roll, face recognition runs on-device (or on the NAS GPU if you have one), and shared albums work across accounts. Runs comfortably on a Synology Plus-series with Docker.
 Where it falls short: Face recognition on CPU is slow for large libraries (10k+ photos) on older DS units. AI model updates occasionally need a re-init step.
 Pricing: 
 Free (AGPL). Optional paid support at immich.app .
 Platforms: Docker.
 Download: Immich.app 
 Bottom line: If Synology Photos is why you keep paying Google, replace both with Immich.
 3. Jellyfin – best media server without Plex
 Jellyfin is the fully open-source media server that has caught up with Plex on the DSM front. Hardware transcoding works on any Synology model with Intel QuickSync (the Plus-series x86 boxes), and the mobile and TV apps are close to Plex’s polish now.
 Where it falls short: No first-party remote-access relay. If you want to stream outside your LAN, you need Tailscale or a reverse proxy. Metadata scraping occasionally misses; manual fixes are quick.
 Pricing: 
 Free (GPL).
 Platforms: Docker; native clients on every major TV and phone platform.
 Download: Jellyfin.org 
 Bottom line: Jellyfin is the “own your media” pick with no paywalls behind any feature.
 4. Homepage – best dashboard for services
 Homepage is the start page every home lab settles on. YAML-driven config for services, live widgets that pull uptime and status from the containers you already run (Portainer, Immich, Jellyfin, Home Assistant, and dozens more), and a search bar that hits DuckDuckGo, Google, or your own SearXNG.
 Where it falls short: No login screen out of the box; put it behind your reverse proxy if the NAS is exposed. Widget errors need a container restart to clear cleanly.
 Pricing: 
 Free (GPL).
 Platforms: Docker.
 Download: gethomepage.dev 
 Bottom line: Homepage is the browser bookmark that replaces “which port was Jellyfin on again?”
 5. Pi-hole – best network-wide ad blocker
 Pi-hole blocks ads and trackers at the DNS layer for every device on the LAN, including smart TVs and consoles that browser extensions cannot touch. Runs happily in a Docker container on the Synology, listens on the standard DNS ports, and reports which client asked for which domain.
 Where it falls short: Container Manager needs the DNS ports mapped explicitly (53/tcp and 53/udp) and Synology’s own DNS service (if enabled) has to move. Not a full firewall.
 Pricing: 
 Free (EUPL).
 Platforms: Docker.
 Download: Pi-hole.net 
 Bottom line: Pi-hole is the container everyone in the house benefits from without knowing you installed it.
 6. Vaultwarden – best self-hosted password manager
 Vaultwarden is a Bitwarden-compatible server written in Rust that fits under 50 MB of RAM. Bitwarden desktop, browser, and mobile clients connect to it exactly as they connect to the official service. You own the vault; sync between devices happens over your LAN or through your own reverse proxy.
 Where it falls short: Backups are your job. A single corrupted volume without a Hyper Backup snapshot means starting over.
 Pricing: 
 Free (GPL).
 Platforms: Docker.
 Download: Vaultwarden GitHub 
 Bottom line: Vaultwarden is the “stop paying for a password manager” move for anyone with a Synology already running.
 7. Paperless-ngx – best document archive with OCR
 Paperless-ngx takes anything you scan or drop into a watch folder, runs OCR, tags it, and files it into an archive with a search that actually works. Pair it with the Synology-attached scanner (many recent DS models expose one via USB) and every receipt, contract, and manual is one search away instead of stacked in the physical filing cabinet.
 Where it falls short: First-run OCR on a large backlog will pin a Synology CPU for hours. Frontend is functional, not fancy.
 Pricing: 
 Free (GPL).
 Platforms: Docker.
 Download: Paperless-ngx docs 
 Bottom line: Paperless-ngx is the “no more physical filing cabinet” upgrade that will save you a Sunday every year.
 How to pick the right one
 If you have not run Docker before , start with Portainer . Everything else assumes it.
 If your reason to buy the Synology was photos , replace Synology Photos with Immich .
 If your reason was media , replace Plex with Jellyfin .
 If you want one page to see everything , Homepage .
 If the household hates ads , Pi-hole .
 If you are paying for 1Password or Bitwarden , Vaultwarden pays for the NAS in a year.
 If the physical filing cabinet is a problem, Paperless-ngx .
 You can run all seven on a DS920+ or better. On a 2-bay value-line unit, pick three; the RAM ceiling bites at four.
 FAQ
 Do I need to disable Synology packages before installing these containers?
 Only when the container replaces a package (Immich vs Synology Photos, Jellyfin vs Video Station, Pi-hole vs Synology DNS Server). Leaving both running works but wastes RAM and confuses backups.
 Where should I store container data on a Synology NAS?
 Create a shared folder called docker and bind-mount container volumes into subfolders. That keeps Hyper Backup working and matches every tutorial you will find. Do not use /volume1/@docker/ directly; that path is a moving target across DSM updates.
 Can I run these containers on an ARM Synology NAS?
 Most, yes. Immich, Jellyfin, Homepage, Pi-hole, Vaultwarden, and Paperless-ngx all publish ARM64 images. Portainer does too. A handful of niche containers are amd64-only; check the image tag before pulling.
 What is the biggest self-hosted container that runs on a Synology NAS?
 Immich is the heaviest of these seven because of its machine-learning image tagging. It fits on a DS920+ with 8 GB of RAM alongside a couple of other containers. Nextcloud (not on this list) is similar. Anything AI-heavy needs an x86 Plus-series box.
 How do I keep Docker containers on a Synology up to date?
 Container Manager can auto-pull latest images and recreate containers on a schedule. Portainer has the same option under Stacks. For finer control, add Watchtower (an eighth container) and let it prune old images too.

 1. Why should you run Jellyfin on a Synology NAS?

 Create the project directory and obtain the current Immich Compose and environment files.
 Rename example.env to .env and set storage paths before importing photos.
 Create a Project in Container Manager pointing to the directory containing docker-compose.yml .
 Start the project and open the web interface on the configured port, commonly 2283 .
 Install the mobile application and configure automatic backup.
 Back up both the original library and the database.
 Immich is not a backup merely because it uploads photographs to the NAS. The database contains important metadata, and machine-learning features can consume substantial CPU, RAM, disk space, and time. Consider placing the database on reliable or SSD storage if your NAS supports that arrangement.
 Do not replace Immich’s Compose file casually during an upgrade. Read the release notes and follow the current Synology procedure first; the current guide calls for backup, stopping and rebuilding the project when appropriate, and checking firewall or container-network communication. Users who want lower maintenance may prefer Synology Photos.
 3. Why is Paperless-ngx useful on a Synology NAS? 
 Paperless-ngx turns receipts, warranties, tax documents, manuals, and scans into a searchable archive. Its advantage over an ordinary shared folder is the document workflow: OCR, tags, correspondents, document types, metadata, and a consumption inbox.
 The Paperless-ngx setup documentation says Docker is the preferred installation route for most users, provides Compose templates, recommends PostgreSQL for new installations, and documents the use of Redis in its Docker Compose setup.
 A practical project layout
 /docker/paperless/
├── consume/
├── data/
├── media/
└── export/ 
 Download the project’s current Compose and environment files.
 Bind-mount persistent locations for documents, media, application data, and the consume directory.
 Set the timezone, secret key, administrator credentials, database settings, and any required UID/GID values.
 Start the project with the documented commands:
 docker compose pull
docker compose up -d 
 The documentation uses port 8000 in its example. Drop a test PDF into the consume folder, then verify that Paperless-ngx imports, OCRs, and makes the document searchable. Treat the consume folder as an inbox, not as the permanent archive.
 Permissions are the most common early problem. Paperless-ngx may not be able to consume files if the container user does not match the NAS permissions. The documentation describes USERMAP_UID and USERMAP_GID settings. Filesystems such as NFS may not provide the inotify notifications Paperless-ngx normally uses; the documentation describes polling for those cases.
 OCR can be slow on low-end CPUs, and a database backup is as important as backing up document files because metadata and search information may otherwise be lost. If you only scan an occasional document, Synology Drive plus a disciplined folder system may be easier to maintain.
 4. Is Vaultwarden safe to run on Synology? 
 Vaultwarden is a lightweight, unofficial Bitwarden-compatible server implementation. Vaultwarden can provide Bitwarden-compatible clients and workflows on a NAS, but Vaultwarden is not the official Bitwarden server and should not be treated as a risk-free replacement for a managed password service.
 Vaultwarden stores persistent information under /data inside the container. Create a bind mount such as:

 The Vaultwarden container guidance explains the persistent data requirement. Enable automatic restart, protect the administration endpoint, and back up the data directory independently.
 Security rules for Vaultwarden
 Do not expose Vaultwarden over plain HTTP.
 Use HTTPS through a correctly configured reverse proxy, or access Vaultwarden privately through a VPN such as Tailscale.
 Use a strong master password and enable multifactor authentication where supported by the account and clients.
 Keep the server patched and read release notes before upgrades.
 Test restoration of the Vaultwarden data before trusting the NAS as the only copy.
 Do not expose DSM, Container Manager, or the database to the public internet alongside Vaultwarden.
 Vaultwarden suits technically confident users who accept responsibility for security, backups, certificates, updates, and account recovery. Hosted Bitwarden, 1Password, or Proton Pass is a better fit when minimizing operational responsibility matters more than self-hosting.
 5. What does AdGuard Home do on Synology? 
 AdGuard Home provides network-wide DNS filtering for advertisements and trackers. DNS filtering can cover smart TVs, game consoles, phones, and other devices that cannot install browser extensions. The official Docker image is adguard/adguardhome .
 The AdGuard Home Docker documentation uses persistent locations for configuration and working data. Initial setup commonly uses port 3000 , although final DNS and web-interface ports depend on configuration and existing Synology services.
 The major design problem is availability: if every household device uses the NAS as its DNS server and the NAS is offline, DNS resolution may fail across the network. Choose at least one fallback strategy:
 Run a second resolver on another device.
 Configure the router with a fallback resolver.
 Apply AdGuard Home only to selected clients initially.
 Enable automatic container restart and verify startup after a NAS reboot.
 Document how to revert DHCP or DNS settings if AdGuard Home fails.
 DNS filtering can break login pages, captive portals, streaming services, smart-home devices, or applications that depend on particular domains. Whitelisting is normal. AdGuard Home does not replace endpoint security or a firewall. Pi-hole, router-based filtering, or managed AdGuard DNS may be easier for a nontechnical household.
 6. Why should Uptime Kuma monitor your Synology containers? 
 Uptime Kuma checks whether the NAS, containerized web services, websites, and network devices remain reachable and sends notifications when a check fails. Uptime Kuma becomes more valuable after installing several services because a container can stop silently even when the NAS itself appears healthy.
 Install Uptime Kuma with a persistent data mount and automatic restart. Create checks for the NAS, Jellyfin, Immich, Paperless-ngx, Vaultwarden, AdGuard Home, internet connectivity, and backup-job status pages where available. Monitor an application URL rather than only an open port when you want to verify that the service actually responds.
 The Uptime Kuma project is suitable for availability monitoring, but it is not a complete replacement for DSM Resource Monitor, SMART health checks, storage scrubbing, backup verification, or a Prometheus/Grafana metrics stack. If the NAS and home internet connection fail together, a hosted monitor such as UptimeRobot or Better Stack can provide an independent alert path.

 Do not create noisy checks that alert during every brief restart. Set sensible intervals and notification rules, then test the notifications by intentionally stopping a noncritical service.
 7. Should you run Nextcloud instead of Synology Drive? 
 Run Nextcloud when you need a private cloud workspace for file synchronization, sharing, calendars, contacts, collaboration, and extensions. Skip Nextcloud when Synology Drive, Synology Photos, and other DSM applications already meet your needs.
 Nextcloud is a multi-component application that typically involves a database and caching services. Updates require more care than a single stateless container, and office collaboration may require additional services such as Collabora or ONLYOFFICE. Use Nextcloud’s official Docker documentation rather than copying an unexplained third-party Compose file.
 Choose Synology Drive when… 
 Choose Nextcloud when… 
 You want the lowest-maintenance file synchronization on a Synology NAS. 
 You need a broader private-cloud workspace and extension ecosystem. 
 You already use DSM accounts, permissions, and native integration. 
 You accept database, caching, upgrade, and recovery responsibilities. 
 You do not need extensive collaboration features. 
 You need features beyond ordinary file sync and sharing. 
 Nextcloud is the most heavily qualified recommendation in this list. Seafile may suit users focused primarily on file synchronization, while a hosted Nextcloud service may be preferable to operating the application yourself.
 Which supporting tools should accompany these containers? 
 Use Tailscale for private remote access
 Tailscale is highly useful alongside these services, but Tailscale is not one of the seven Docker containers. Tailscale provides an official Synology package, so installing it through DSM is often more appropriate than adding another container. Its Synology integration documentation notes that DSM 7 may require additional configuration for outbound access from other applications.
 Prefer local-only access for services that do not need to be remote. Use Tailscale or another VPN for private access. Publish a service through an HTTPS reverse proxy only when you understand DNS, certificates, authentication, patching, and exposure risks. Never expose DSM, Container Manager, databases, Vaultwarden administration, or AdGuard Home administration directly to the public internet.
 Use snapshots and independent backups
 Snapshots provide convenient point-in-time recovery when the NAS uses a suitable filesystem, but snapshots remain on the NAS unless replicated elsewhere. Hyper Backup or another backup system should copy important data to an independent destination.
 Independent reader support Your contribution helps us test, update, and keep practical guides available for everyone. Support on Ko-Fi How should you update Docker projects safely? 
 The commands docker compose pull and docker compose up -d are common Compose update steps, but they are not a universal upgrade procedure. Follow the application’s documented migration path first, especially for Immich, Paperless-ngx, and Nextcloud.
 Back up the application data and database.
 Save the Compose file and protect the environment file containing secrets.
 Read the project changelog and migration instructions.
 Update one project at a time.
 Pull the documented image versions rather than blindly tracking latest .
 Recreate or rebuild only as the project instructs.
 Check logs for database migrations, permission errors, and failed dependencies.
 Test the web interface, mobile clients, uploads, searches, and authentication.
 Confirm that Uptime Kuma sees the service as healthy.
 Verify that backup jobs still run and that mount paths were not accidentally changed.
 Keep Compose files and environment files in backed-up, versioned storage. Do not assume a successful container restart proves that the data is persistent or recoverable.
 Also popular on Amazon

 What should you back up? 
 Back up the information needed to recreate both the containers and their data. For each project, preserve its Compose file, environment settings with secrets protected, image or version notes, application configuration, databases, and user libraries.

 RAID protects availability against some disk failures; RAID does not protect against deletion, corruption, ransomware, theft, or destruction of the NAS. A second folder on the same NAS is not an independent backup. Perform at least one restore test so that recovery is demonstrated rather than assumed.
 Which NAS containers are best for different hardware?

 Installing Nextcloud merely because it is popular

 Exposing administration panels directly to the internet 
 What is the best four-container starting point? 
 For most capable Synology NAS owners, the best initial selection is Jellyfin for media, Immich for photos, Paperless-ngx for documents, and Vaultwarden for passwords. Add Uptime Kuma as soon as several services are running. Add AdGuard Home only after planning DNS fallback, and add Nextcloud only when its collaboration features justify another multi-component application.
 Frequently Asked Questions 
 Can every Synology NAS run these seven Docker containers?
 No. Container Manager availability depends on the Synology model and DSM version, while performance depends on CPU architecture, RAM, storage, and workload. Older ARM NAS models may be suitable for Vaultwarden, AdGuard Home, and Uptime Kuma but may struggle with Immich, OCR, databases, or Jellyfin transcoding.
 Is Container Manager the same as Docker on Synology?
 Container Manager is Synology’s DSM application for managing Docker containers and Compose projects. Container Manager provides the Synology interface, while each application still has its own image, mount paths, environment variables, dependencies, and upgrade instructions.
 Should I install all seven containers?
 No. Choose containers based on recurring needs and available hardware. A modest NAS may be better served by three or four services, because Immich, Jellyfin transcoding, Nextcloud, and OCR-heavy Paperless-ngx can compete for CPU, memory, storage I/O, and database resources.
 Is Vaultwarden the official Bitwarden server?
 No. Vaultwarden is an unofficial Bitwarden-compatible server implementation. Vaultwarden can be useful for technically capable users, but hosted Bitwarden or another managed password manager reduces the responsibility for HTTPS, patching, backups, account recovery, and outage planning.
 Can I access Synology Docker containers remotely without port forwarding?
 Yes. Tailscale or another VPN can provide private remote access without publishing every service through router port forwarding. Tailscale is commonly installed as an official Synology package rather than counted as one of the seven Docker containers.
 The Bottom Line 
 Bottom line: The best Docker containers you should run on your Synology NAS are the ones that solve specific recurring problems without exceeding the NAS’s hardware or your maintenance capacity. Start with Jellyfin, Immich, Paperless-ngx, or Vaultwarden according to your needs; use Uptime Kuma for visibility, plan AdGuard Home’s DNS fallback, and treat Nextcloud as an optional private-cloud project rather than a default installation.

Overview Paperless-ngx provides OCR, indexing, tagging and full-text search over the household's scanned documents. It runs in a dedicated unprivileged Debian 13 LXC (CT 126 carn ) on cluster node pve3 , chosen for OCR throughput — the MS-02's Core Ultra 9 285HX processes OCRmyPDF far faster than the Gen10 Opterons. The design keeps the irreplaceable document archive on ZFS ( tank/storage , inside the existing sanoid → syncoid → restic pipeline) while keeping the regenerable search index on the container's local rootfs. Documents reach Paperless by two routes: the Paperless API (Paperless Mobile app, direct), and a watched consume folder shared with Nextcloud over SMB so any household member can drop a scan without extra software. Access is internal + Tailscale only. No inbound router port; no Cloudflare Tunnel. Why this design? Placement on pve3 — OCR is CPU-bound; the Ultra 9 clears a multi-page journal PDF in ~1.7s versus far longer on the Opterons. Native install, not Docker-in-LXC — the community-scripts helper installs Paperless, Redis and PostgreSQL directly in the CT, avoiding a nested container runtime. Documents on ZFS, index local — the media tree (originals + OCR archive) is irreplaceable and goes on tank/storage ; the Whoosh search index is regenerable ( document_index reindex ) and stays off NFS to avoid file-locking and corruption over the wire. NFS bridge to the storage anchor — tank is local to pve ; CT 126 is on pve3. Documents cross the 10 GbE storage fabric via an NFS 4.2 export (the same pattern as CT 122 binnian /Plex), all-squashed to a single consistent owner. One owner model — the NFS export and the Samba family share both resolve document writes to ncsvc:familydata ( 100999:101001 on the host), so the API path and the Nextcloud path write identically-owned files. 2. Architecture 2.1 Components Component Host IP Notes Paperless-ngx CT 126 carn (Debian 13 LXC, unprivileged) granian :8000; Redis; PostgreSQL — all native in the CT Storage anchor pve — ZFS tank/storage/Paperless / storage Exported over NFS 4.2 on the storage fabric NFS transport pve → pve3 over /24 (MTU 9000) — mnt-paperless.mount systemd unit on pve3 Nextcloud VM 111 mweelrea External SMB mount "Scans" (id 28) → family/Paperless/consume NAS / Samba CT 101 oriel family share = /mnt/storage ; serves the consume drop path DNS CT 106 commedagh (Pi-hole primary) CT 126 resolver 2.2 CT 126 specification VMID / hostname 126 / carn Template debian-13-standard_13.1-2_amd64.tar.zst Type Unprivileged LXC, nesting=1 , keyctl=1 CPU / RAM 4 cores / 4096 MiB Rootfs vmstorage:subvol-126-disk-0 , 12 GB Network eth0 on vmbr0 , IP /24 , gw DNS (commedagh) Mountpoint mp0: /mnt/paperless,mp=/mnt/paperless (NFS-backed bind) Timezone Europe/London Node pve3 2.3 Data-flow diagram flowchart LR subgraph clients["Clients"] MOB["Paperless Mobile

Storage design 3.1 Directory layout on pve Created as plain directories under tank/storage (not a child dataset) so they inherit the existing restic scope with zero exclude/include changes — tank/storage is already the restic target. install -d -m 2770 -o 100999 -g 101001 \ /tank/storage/Paperless \ /tank/storage/Paperless/consume \ /tank/storage/Paperless/media \ /tank/storage/Paperless/export Ownership 100999:101001 is the host-mapped view of container ncsvc:familydata (999:1001). Mode 2770 (setgid) makes new files inherit the familydata group. Path Purpose On ZFS? Backed up? Paperless/consume Watched drop folder (Nextcloud writes here) Yes Yes (transient) Paperless/media OCR'd archive + originals — irreplaceable Yes Yes Paperless/export On-demand document dumps Yes Yes PAPERLESS_DATA_DIR → /opt/paperless_data/data Whoosh index, models No (CT rootfs) No — regenerable 3.2 NFS export ( /etc/exports on pve) /tank/storage/Paperless (rw,sync,no_subtree_check,all_squash,anonuid=100999,anongid=101001) all_squash with anonuid/anongid forces every write (regardless of the calling uid inside the CT, which runs Paperless as root) to land as 100999:101001 on ZFS. This is what makes the API path and the SMB path write identically-owned files. is pve3's storage-fabric address. Applied with exportfs -ra ; verified with exportfs -v . 3.3 systemd mount on pve3 /etc/systemd/system/mnt-paperless.mount — mirrors the existing mnt-media.mount unit, with an added [Install] section so it auto-mounts on boot (the media unit relies on an external pull; this one enables cleanly): [Unit] Description =NFS mount of tank/storage/Paperless from pve (10GbE) After =network-online.target Wants =network-online.target [Mount] What =:/tank/storage/Paperless Where =/mnt/paperless Type =nfs4 Options = nfsvers =4.2,hard, proto =tcp,noatime,_netdev [Install] WantedBy =multi-user.target systemctl daemon-reload systemctl enable --now mnt-paperless.mount 3.4 Bind-mount into CT 126 pct set 126 -mp0 /mnt/paperless,mp=/mnt/paperless pct reboot 126 Inside the unprivileged CT the mounted files appear owned 999 1001 (the container-relative view of the squashed host ids). Writes through the mount land on ZFS as 100999:101001 . Verified with a root-in-CT touch test returning 999 1001 . 4. Build procedure 4.1 Create the container Community-scripts paperless-ngx helper, run in Advanced mode: bash -c " $( curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/community-scripts/ProxmoxVE/main/ct/paperless-ngx.sh ) " Advanced settings entered: Unprivileged · CTID 126 · hostname carn · disk 12 GB · 4 cores · 4096 MB · bridge vmbr0 · IP /24 · gw · DNS · storage vmstorage · node pve3. Adminer declined. Helper output confirms four services created and the URL http://carn.:8000 . 4.2 Admin password The helper sets an admin password but does not persist it to a creds file on this build. Reset to a known value (stored in Vaultwarden) via uv run (this build runs the service as root, not a paperless user, and uses uv , not a plain venv): cd /opt/paperless/src && uv run -- python manage.py changepassword admin 4.3 Fix the granian bind (IPv6 → IPv4) Symptom: ERR_EMPTY_RESPONSE / "didn't send any data" from a browser, but curl to 127.0.0.1:8000 and to :8000 from the host both return 302 . Cause: the webserver unit sets Environment=GRANIAN_HOST=:: (IPv6 wildcard). This CT was created with IPv6: none , so IPv4-mapped-on-v6 does not work and external IPv4 clients get an empty response. Fix: pct exec 126 -- cp /etc/systemd/system/paperless-webserver.service{,.bak} pct exec 126 -- sed -i ' s/^Environment=GRANIAN_HOST=::/Environment=GRANIAN_HOST=0.0.0.0/ ' \ /etc/systemd/system/paperless-webserver.service pct exec 126 -- systemctl daemon-reload pct exec 126 -- systemctl restart paperless-webserver pct exec 126 -- ss -tlnp | grep 8000 # expect 0.0.0.0:8000 4.4 Repoint the document directories Back up the conf, then repoint consume/media onto the NFS mount and add the NFS-polling behaviour. PAPERLESS_DATA_DIR is deliberately left on local rootfs. pct exec 126 -- cp /opt/paperless/paperless.conf{,.bak} pct exec 126 -- sed -i \ -e ' s#^PAPERLESS_CONSUMPTION_DIR=/opt/paperless_data/consume#PAPERLESS_CONSUMPTION_DIR=/mnt/paperless/consume# ' \ -e ' s#^PAPERLESS_MEDIA_ROOT=/opt/paperless_data/media#PAPERLESS_MEDIA_ROOT=/mnt/paperless/media# ' \ /opt/paperless/paperless.conf Appended block: # --- NFS-backed consume dir: poll instead of inotify --- PAPERLESS_CONSUMER_POLLING=5 PAPERLESS_CONSUMER_RECURSIVE=true PAPERLESS_CONSUMER_IGNORE_PATTERNS=[".DS_STORE/*", "._*", ".stfolder/*", ".stversions/*", ".localized/*", "desktop.ini", "@eaDir/*"] CONSUMER_POLLING=5 is mandatory: inotify events are not delivered reliably across NFS, so the consumer must poll. Restart all four services: pct exec 126 -- systemctl restart paperless-webserver paperless-consumer paperless-scheduler paperless-task-queue 4.5 Harden pct exec 126 -- chmod 600 /opt/paperless/paperless.conf # protects PAPERLESS_SECRET_KEY Set the canonical URL (drives ALLOWED_HOSTS and CSRF_TRUSTED_ORIGINS ; local A record carn. → must exist first): pct exec 126 -- bash -c ' echo "PAPERLESS_URL=http://carn.:8000" >> /opt/paperless/paperless.conf ' pct exec 126 -- systemctl restart paperless-webserver Widen accepted hostnames for LAN + Tailscale access (else the tailnet name returns 400 DisallowedHost ; CSRF_TRUSTED_ORIGINS is required for login over any non-canonical name — it needs scheme + port, ALLOWED_HOSTS is host-only): PAPERLESS_ALLOWED_HOSTS=carn.,carn..ts.net,, PAPERLESS_CSRF_TRUSTED_ORIGINS=http://carn.:8000,http://carn..ts.net:8000,http://:8000,http://:8000 Remote access (travelling): the Tailscale MagicDNS name carn..ts.net:8000 is the robust path — no split-DNS or subnet-router dependency, and avoids the .local mDNS interception some clients apply. The local-domain path also works over Tailscale if a restricted nameserver for the local zone is set in the tailnet DNS config and the LAN subnet route is approved. Prefer the ts.net name for travel. 4.6 Verify (isolated drop test) Drop a PDF directly into /mnt/paperless/consume from the pve3 host and watch the task queue: pct exec 126 -- journalctl -u paperless-task-queue --since ' -90s ' --no-pager | tail -20 Expect Success. New document id N created and media/documents/{originals,archive,thumbnails} created on the NFS mount owned 999 1001 . 5. Nextcloud ingest integration Adds one external-storage SMB mount pointing at the consume dir via the existing family share, scoped to group managers (household admins only — Clare and Richard, not the children). Run on VM 111 mweelrea ( occ shell). Substitute the real ncsvc password from Keeper/Vaultwarden: ID= $( occ files_external:create " Scans " smb password::password 2> /dev/null | grep -oE ' [0-9]+$ ' ) occ files_external:config " $ID " host < NAS-IP > occ files_external:config " $ID " share family occ files_external:config " $ID " root " Paperless/consume " occ files_external:config " $ID " user ncsvc occ files_external:config " $ID " password ' ' occ files_external:applicable " $ID " --remove-all occ files_external:applicable " $ID " --add-group managers occ files_external:option " $ID " enable_sharing false occ files_external:option " $ID " previews false occ files_external:verify " $ID " Mount id assigned: 28 . verify returns status: ok, code: 0 . Two deliberate options: previews false (a transient drop folder needs no thumbnail cache — avoids the known local disk-fill regrowth) and --add-group managers (scope). The privacy lever is --remove-all then --add-group ; without it the mount is global. Permissions alignment: the consume dir is 100999:101001 mode 2770 ; the family Samba share uses force user = ncsvc, force group = familydata . SMB writes therefore land as ncsvc:familydata — identical to what the NFS all_squash path writes. One consistent owner across both access paths. Verified end-to-end: a PDF uploaded to the Scans folder in the Nextcloud browser flowed through SMB → ZFS → NFS → consumer → OCR → document id 2 on ZFS (originals + archive present, owned 999 1001 ). 6. Client upload paths Path For whom Mechanism Works remotely? Paperless Mobile (F-Droid / Play) Richard (power user) Direct Paperless API to carn.:8000 ; Android share target from any app Yes, over Tailscale Nextcloud "Scans" folder Clare + managers SMB drop → consume folder → consumer ingest Yes (Nextcloud is Cloudflare-fronted) Scanner app → Nextcloud folder Any household member Scanner outputs PDF to the Scans folder Yes Host drop Richard (admin/testing) cp into /mnt/paperless/consume on pve3 LAN/Tailscale Paperless-ngx has no official Android app; Paperless Mobile is the community client and is the recommended day-to-day tool for the maintainer. The Nextcloud route is the no-extra-software household path. 7. Known quirks and gotchas Quirk Detail GRANIAN_HOST=:: on IPv6-disabled CTs Community-scripts default binds the IPv6 wildcard; on IPv6: none guests this yields ERR_EMPTY_RESPONSE for IPv4 browsers. Set 0.0.0.0 . Applies to any community-scripts granian guest. Web UI on port 8000 , not 8080 This build serves on 8000; older guides assume 8080. Browser HTTPS-upgrade Chrome/Edge "Always use secure connections" / HSTS rewrites http://:8000 to https:// , TLS-handshakes a plaintext port → ERR_EMPTY_RESPONSE . Not an infra fault. Use incognito or disable the toggle / clear HSTS at chrome://net-internals/#hsts . Service user is root , uses uv No paperless service user on this build; manage.py runs via uv run . Data paths are /opt/paperless_data/{consume,data,media} Not /opt/paperless/… as some guides state. NFS + inotify inotify is unreliable over NFS; CONSUMER_POLLING=5 is mandatory for the watched dir. Search index must stay off NFS Whoosh over NFS invites locking/corruption; keep DATA_DIR on local rootfs. PAPERLESS_URL needs a DNS record Set to http://carn.:8000 (local A record required first). Also drives ALLOWED_HOSTS + CSRF_TRUSTED_ORIGINS . Must include the :8000 port (no reverse proxy). 8. Operational runbook 8.1 Service health pct exec 126 -- systemctl is-active paperless-webserver paperless-consumer paperless-scheduler paperless-task-queue pct exec 126 -- ss -tlnp | grep 8000 8.2 Watch a consume run pct exec 126 -- journalctl -u paperless-consumer -f # detection pct exec 126 -- journalctl -u paperless-task-queue -f # OCR + filing 8.3 Rebuild the search index (after a restore or corruption) pct exec 126 -- bash -c ' cd /opt/paperless/src && uv run -- python manage.py document_index reindex ' 8.4 Manual document export pct exec 126 -- bash -c ' cd /opt/paperless/src && uv run -- python manage.py document_exporter /mnt/paperless/export ' 8.5 Updates Snapshot the CT first, then run the community-scripts update entrypoint ( update from the CT), or the in-tree manage.py migrate path per Paperless release notes. Read notes before major version jumps. 9. Troubleshooting Symptom Cause Fix Browser ERR_EMPTY_RESPONSE , curl returns 302 granian on IPv6 wildcard, or browser HTTPS-upgrade §4.3 (bind fix); or incognito / clear HSTS File dropped in Scans never appears in consume SMB write not reaching backend, or Nextcloud scan lag occ files:scan --path="/richard/files/Scans" ; check mount root is Paperless/consume File in consume but never consumed Consumer not polling / wrong path Confirm CONSUMER_POLLING=5 and CONSUMPTION_DIR=/mnt/paperless/consume ; restart consumer Truncated/corrupt document from SMB drop File consumed mid-write Raise the consumer's unmodified-file wait; Paperless's default readiness check normally covers this OCR fails with language error Missing tesseract language pack Install tesseract-ocr- in the CT; default is English verify → status error, code 1 Placeholder password left in mount config occ files_external:config password '' , re-verify Mount not present after pve3 reboot Unit not enabled Confirm [Install] section + systemctl enable mnt-paperless.mount 10. Backup and restore Media ( tank/storage/Paperless/media ) rides the existing restic off-site run automatically — it is under tank/storage , the restic target, with no include/exclude change required. Index ( DATA_DIR ) is not backed up and is rebuilt with document_index reindex after a restore. Verify capture after the next scheduled run: tail -n 5 /var/log/restic-offsite.log restic snapshots latest --path /tank/storage | tail -3 Restore drill: restore media from restic (or the peer ZFS replica), point a fresh Paperless at it via MEDIA_ROOT , then document_index reindex to rebuild search. The PostgreSQL database (document metadata, tags, correspondents) is inside the CT — include the CT in vzdump/PBS so metadata and media restore together. Note: media on ZFS covers the files . The Paperless database (tags, dates, correspondents, document↔file mapping) lives in the CT's PostgreSQL. A media-only restore without the DB gives you files with no index metadata. Ensure CT 126 is in the vzdump/PBS job. 11. Family usage Household members drop scans into the Scans folder in Nextcloud (visible to managers). Anything dropped there is OCR'd, dated and filed automatically, and becomes full-text searchable in the Paperless web UI at http://carn.:8000 . Richard additionally uses Paperless Mobile to push documents straight from his phone, including when away (via Tailscale). 12. Explain like I'm 5 There's a magic in-tray. Put any letter or receipt into the "Scans" box on the family cloud, and a little robot reads it, works out what it says and when it's from, and files it in a big searchable cabinet — so later you can find "that letter from the council" by just typing a word from it. The cabinet lives on the big safe disk that gets copied to Germany every night, so nothing is ever lost. 13. References Paperless-ngx documentation — configuration, consumer, exporter, reindex. Proxmox VE Administration Guide — unprivileged LXC, bind mounts ( pct set -mpN ), user-namespace id mapping. nextcloud-family-storage-INTERNAL.md — the files_external scoping pattern and family share model reused here. proxmox-infrastructure-INTERNAL.md — cluster topology, storage fabric, the CT 122 binnian NFS pattern this build mirrors. community-scripts ProxmoxVE — paperless-ngx helper. End of INTERNAL runbook. Sanitised public counterpart: paperless-ngx-PUBLIC.md . You can’t perform that action at this time.

 # docker-compose.yml: Single-file Paperless-ngx deployment for Docker Compose, 
 # Synology Container Manager, and Portainer. 
 # 
 # Services included: 
 # - redis: https://hub.docker.com/_/redis 
 # - postgres: https://hub.docker.com/_/postgres 
 # - gotenberg: https://github.com/gotenberg/gotenberg 
 # - tika: https://tika.apache.org 
 # - paperless-ngx: https://github.com/paperless-ngx/paperless-ngx 
 # - paperless-ai: https://github.com/clusterzx/paperless-ai

 # 
 # Setup default properties for all containers. 
 # 
 x-default-container : &default-container # YAML anchor for default container settings 
 pull_policy : always # Pull the configured image before recreation 
 restart : unless-stopped # Restart unless an operator explicitly stops it 
 security_opt : # Apply container runtime security options 
 - no-new-privileges:true # Prevent processes from gaining new privileges 
 logging : # Configure bounded JSON container logs 
 driver : json-file # Use Docker's JSON file logging driver 
 options : # Configure log rotation limits 
 max-size : ${LOG_MAX_SIZE} # Maximum size of each rotated log file 
 max-file : ${LOG_MAX_FILE} # Maximum number of log files retained 
 # 
 # Labels for containers that should not be updated unattended by Watchtower. 
 # 
 # Paperless-ngx upgrades can include database migrations and coordinated image 
 # changes. Update the stack intentionally after reviewing release notes and the 
 # repository upgrade guide. 
 # 
 x-disable-watchtower-updates : &disable-watchtower-updates # Disable unattended Watchtower updates 
 - " com.centurylinklabs.watchtower.enable=false " # Require intentional updates for this container 
 # 
 # Define the services used in this stack. 
 # 
 services :
 # 
 # Configure the Redis-compatible broker used by Paperless background workers. 
 # 
 redis :
 # Docker image and container information 
 << : *default-container # Pull in default container settings 
 image : redis:${REDIS_TAG} # Use the short name for Synology image tracking 
 container_name : redis-${REDIS_TAG} # Append the image tag to the container name 
 hostname : redis # Set the internal service hostname 
 user : ${DEFAULT_UID}:${DEFAULT_GID} # Run with the configured host identity 
 read_only : true # Keep the container root filesystem read-only 
 # Tune the broker connection queue 
 sysctls :
 - net.core.somaxconn=512 # Permit the expected broker connection backlog 
 # Start Redis with authenticated client access 
 command :
 - redis-server # Start the Redis server process 
 - --requirepass # Require clients to authenticate 
 - ${REDIS_PASSWORD} # Use the configured broker password 
 # Apply container labels 
 labels : *disable-watchtower-updates # Update the broker intentionally with the stack 
 # Define the container environment 
 environment :
 TZ : ${TZ} # Set the container timezone 
 REDISCLI_AUTH : ${REDIS_PASSWORD} # Authenticate redis-cli health checks 
 # Mount persistent broker data 
 volumes :
 - ${REDIS_CONFIG_PATH}:/data:rw # Redis persistence directory 
 # Report healthy when the authenticated broker responds 
 healthcheck :
 test : # Ping Redis through the bundled client 
 - CMD 
 - redis-cli 
 - ping 
 timeout : ${REDIS_HEALTHCHECK_TIMEOUT} # Fail if the check exceeds this duration 
 interval : ${REDIS_HEALTHCHECK_INTERVAL} # Run the check at this interval 
 retries : ${REDIS_HEALTHCHECK_RETRIES} # Mark unhealthy after this many failures 
 # 
 # Configure PostgreSQL for Paperless metadata and application state. 
 # 
 # PostgreSQL 17 and earlier use /var/lib/postgresql/data. PostgreSQL 18 and 
 # later use /var/lib/postgresql. Keep the image major version, mount target, 
 # and on-disk database migration synchronized. 
 # 
 postgres :
 # Docker image and container information 
 << : *default-container # Pull in default container settings 
 image : postgres:${POSTGRES_TAG} # Use the short name for Synology image tracking 
 container_name : postgres-${POSTGRES_TAG} # Append the image tag to the container name 
 hostname : postgres # Set the internal database hostname 
 # Apply container labels 
 labels : *disable-watchtower-updates # Update the database intentionally with the stack 
 # Define the container environment 
 environment :
 POSTGRES_DB : ${POSTGRES_DB} # Create the Paperless database 
 POSTGRES_USER : ${POSTGRES_USER} # Create the Paperless database user 
 POSTGRES_PASSWORD : ${POSTGRES_PASSWORD} # Set the Paperless database password 
 # Mount persistent database state 
 volumes :
 - ${POSTGRES_CONFIG_PATH}:${POSTGRES_DATA_TARGET}:rw # Version-appropriate database directory 
 # Report healthy when the configured database accepts connections 
 healthcheck :
 test : # Query PostgreSQL readiness without printing secrets 
 - CMD 
 - pg_isready 
 - -q 
 - -d 
 - ${POSTGRES_DB} 
 - -U 
 - ${POSTGRES_USER} 
 timeout : ${POSTGRES_HEALTHCHECK_TIMEOUT} # Fail if the check exceeds this duration 
 interval : ${POSTGRES_HEALTHCHECK_INTERVAL} # Run the check at this interval 
 retries : ${POSTGRES_HEALTHCHECK_RETRIES} # Mark unhealthy after this many failures 
 # 
 # Configure Gotenberg to convert Office and email content into PDF files. 
 # 
 gotenberg :
 # Docker image and container information 
 << : *default-container # Pull in default container settings 
 image : gotenberg/gotenberg:${GOTENBERG_TAG} # Run the reviewed Gotenberg image version 
 container_name : gotenberg-${GOTENBERG_TAG} # Append the image tag to the container name 
 hostname : gotenberg # Set the internal conversion service hostname 
 # Disable browser JavaScript while allowing local conversion inputs 
 command :
 - gotenberg # Start the Gotenberg service 
 - --chromium-disable-javascript=true # Disable JavaScript during document conversion 
 - --chromium-allow-list=file:///tmp/.* # Permit temporary local conversion inputs 
 # Apply container labels 
 labels : *disable-watchtower-updates # Update the converter intentionally with the stack 
 # Report healthy when the conversion API responds successfully 
 healthcheck :
 test : # Request the upstream application health endpoint 
 - CMD 
 - curl 
 - -fsS 
 - --max-time 
 - " 2 " 
 - http://127.0.0.1:3000/health 
 timeout : ${GOTENBERG_HEALTHCHECK_TIMEOUT} # Fail if the check exceeds this duration 
 interval : ${GOTENBERG_HEALTHCHECK_INTERVAL} # Run the check at this interval 
 start_period : ${GOTENBERG_HEALTHCHECK_START_PERIOD} # Allow conversion engines to initialize 
 retries : ${GOTENBERG_HEALTHCHECK_RETRIES} # Mark unhealthy after this many failures 
 # 
 # Configure Apache Tika to extract text and metadata from Office documents. 
 # 
 tika :
 # Docker image and container information 
 << : *default-container # Pull in default container settings

 container_name : tika-${TIKA_TAG} # Append the image tag to the container name

 labels : *disable-watchtower-updates # Update the extractor intentionally with the stack

 paperless-ngx :

 << : *default-container # Pull in default container settings
